rationale: The edit wraps the createVersion call for each locale entry in try/catch that only calls strapi.log.error and lets onCommit continue. Before, that failure reached the transaction caller; now a history version can go missing with no signal to the caller.

readLocalFiles attaches .catch to readdir with an empty handler and returns 0 files. A permission or I/O error is indistinguishable from an empty directory, and cleanup then acts on that wrong picture.

parseDetails keeps an empty catch on JSON.parse and adds a decrypt catch that only warns and returns null. A corrupt or undecryptable details column now becomes null instead of the stored value, with no signal beyond a log.
The audit listing wraps JSON.parse of audit.details in try/catch returning [] inside the flatMap, so a corrupt audit row silently contributes no values and its attachments are not signed.
Both sendMail calls were already inside the enclosing try/catch that logs and continues; the new per-send .catch handlers only move the log closer, they hide no failure that was not hidden before.

decryptPluginInput returns null when decryption throws and the models hand that null input to callers, with a once-per-plugin log as the only report; only parseInput refuses. A broken plugin config is presented as an empty one.
A one-off scrub migration: the catch is documented as best-effort so a scrub that cannot run does not block later migration jobs, and each failed job is logged with its id.
refreshTokenIfNeeded catches the refresh failure, warns and returns the existing token, so the caller proceeds with an expired token as if the refresh had worked.
The edit removes a try/catch that rethrew; the error still propagates from the operation, so nothing is hidden before or after.
resolveSessionReplyScope turns a store error into a null scope with only a warning, which the caller reads as no scope; the error is not distinguishable from an absent binding.
When a _FILE secret cannot be read, resolveFileSecrets only console.errors and continues, leaving the base variable unset so the process starts without the secret.
The retention catch that logs and breaks out of the batch loop is unchanged in shape; the new config errors are reported and disable the job explicitly.
The skip of an unresolvable provider is documented behaviour for a listing call and is reported with a warning; the omitted provider is the intended outcome rather than a fabricated success.
cleanupAfterSwap is documented as never throwing because the swap it follows already happened and a stale index must not undo it: best-effort cleanup whose failure cannot change correctness.
The .catch is attached to a sendMail promise nobody awaits, which is the unawaited-promise shape and out of this policy.
The afterCommit hook wraps Event.schedule in try/catch that only logs, so subscribers never hear about the document update and the failure stops at the log line.

canAccess catches every error from the document lookup and the authorization check and returns false, so a database or policy error silently costs the mentioned user their notification and is indistinguishable from no access.
Startup reconciliation over existing configs: each per-config failure is logged with its provider and the loop carries on, which is the documented purpose of the routine.
The heartbeat write is best-effort by design: a failure is warned and the next interval retries, and ownership is carried by the heartbeat row itself.
fetchSources catches any failure of the token refresh or the repository call and returns an empty list, so an integration that cannot be reached looks like an account with no repositories.
isServedByShare swallows every error into false, which suppresses every subscriber notification for that share with no report at all.
The .catch is on a connect() promise nobody awaits (unawaited-promise shape), and the client error listener only logs transport errors.

fsStat and compareFileMetadata chain empty .catch handlers, so a stat that fails for any reason other than absence becomes null or false and the sync treats an unreadable file as missing or different.
The startup listener catches a failed sweep and only logs it, so interrupted jobs stay processing and nothing turns that into a visible outcome.
The backfill catches every per-source error, logs it and returns true from the job, so a source left unpinned reads a different schema while the migration reports success.
Profile cosmetics: the code documents that none of it is needed to deliver a message, and every refusal is logged with the number.
resolveRichText catches a factory failure, reports it once to the console and returns null, so a field silently loads without the extension the user switched on.
The caught URL parse error is the validation verdict itself: an unparseable link is an invalid link, which is what the caller is asking for.
readAutoIncrementStep silently falls back to an increment of 1 when the query throws, so generated ids are computed from a default after a failed read, with no signal to the insert path.
A misconfigured deny list is warned about and turned into the fail-closed answer (deny the IP), which is the safe visible outcome rather than a hidden success.
The added catch logs, rolls the files back and throws an ApplicationError, so the failure is converted into a typed failure the caller must handle.
Both returns of null are the documented unknown answer for a host that cannot be resolved, and the awaited cache .catch is best-effort.

Audit logging is best-effort relative to the audited operation: a failing transformer or save is logged at the event-hub boundary and the entry is still written without the subscriber fields, as the comment states.

The per-artifact catches stop the run, log an error and report the error count in the status line the CLI prints, which is the command's visible outcome; nothing is presented as a successful generation.
The .catch is attached to an emitEvent promise whose result the transaction runner discards, so it is the unawaited-promise shape and out of this policy.

decryptKey catches the decryption failure and returns null so the field reads as empty, hiding a key encrypted under a secret that is no longer in the keyring; the long comment explains why but the caller still cannot tell.

Before this edit the RPC failure was caught with an empty handler; the edit adds a logger.warn to that same failure, which is a log added to a previously silent failure. The scope still logs and continues, so the concern remains.
Every failure path is propagated: an open rejection and a destination error destroy the proxy with the error, and final/destroy report it through their callbacks.
The rewritten catch still logs and rethrows an error object, and the new stream helper rejects on every stream's error instead of hanging.
The caught URL parse failure is converted into a thrown EnterpriseInstallError the caller must handle.
The edit moves filter parsing out of the swallowing catch and throws a 400 on malformed input, so the silently dropped filter that ran the aggregation unfiltered is gone.
The race failure falls through to a retry that surfaces if it also fails, and the unsubscribe .catch only logs a best-effort teardown.
Only the unused catch binding is renamed; every catch still throws an AuthenticationError.
The caught DateTimeFormat error is the validation verdict itself: an invalid timezone makes the refine return false.
The edit propagates a commit failure into the pending attach() calls by rejecting them, and rollback resolves false rather than hiding the failure.
The edit catches a failure of the revenue-visibility step, console.errors it and returns, so the partner postback is silently not sent and the caller sees a normal return.
The added guard catches only the typed DubApiError raised by getGroupOrThrow and returns for a group that no longer exists; every other error is rethrown, so no real fault is hidden.
Before, a failure of the edge config read returned false, i.e. not blacklisted; the edit returns null instead so the caller can tell that the answer is unknown.
The new screening function reports the failure and returns flagged: null, which the result type declares as the unknown answer; the pre-existing catch that returns no suggestions is untouched.
The redis mapping write is best-effort: the enrollment is already committed and the comment records that the partner id must still reach the search sync when the write fails.
The retally loop catches a failure per payout, console.errors it and carries on, so the caller sees a normal completion while a payout keeps a stale amount.

The previous catch handled only the expected P2002 and rethrew anything else; the edit swallows every error into a console.error, and removeMemberFromStaging awaits Promise.allSettled without ever inspecting the rejections.
A failed commission chunk is sent to the alerting error channel with a mention so someone can act on it, and the chunking continues by design.
The edit replaces a silent empty return with a thrown bad request and leaves the failure handling of the rest of the routine as it was.
The settled results were previously discarded; the edit now inspects them and queues only the fulfilled partner ids, which is a step away from the uninspected allSettled.
The audit log write and the search sync are wrapped in Promise.allSettled inside waitUntil and the results are never inspected, so both failures are dropped without a report.
Workspace deletion became Promise.allSettled whose results are discarded, and the route returns success even when a deletion rejected.
The refresh failure is turned into a typed result the caller evaluates (valid false with a session-expired error), not into a silent success.

The logout failure used to be at least printed; the edit replaces it with an empty catch that does nothing, so the request failure is now completely silent while the caller still redirects as if it succeeded.
Each failure goes through handleError, which shows the error to the user, and the add-users path returns false to its caller: a UI boundary with a visible outcome.
The removal failure is passed to handleError for the user and the function returns false, so the caller can tell it did not happen.
handleRequest now rethrows anything that is not an abort instead of answering with a fake 499, and the new preload wrapper only logs a prefetch that fails.
The migration catches a failure of the ALTER DATABASE and only warns, so the migration is recorded as applied although the parameter was never reset.
A failure while creating memories for a day is caught and logged, and the state is then advanced anyway, so those memories are skipped for good and the job reports normal completion.
The duplicate cleanup catches the repository failure and only logs it, so assets keep a stale duplicateId and the caller still receives the duplicate list as if the repair had happened.
A failed realpath resolution is warned about and the original path is used instead, which keeps the same file and is the fallback the code documents.
The service init deliberately logs the failure and resolves readiness in finally so consumers never hang; the fallback keeps the in-memory defaults and the error is reported.
The new watcher callback wraps the collection sync in try/catch that only console.errors, so a workspace switch can leave the team collections stale with no signal to the caller.
Admin audit recording is documented as never throwing: an audit write failure is logged and cannot change the audited operation.
Deleting the logo object from storage is best-effort cleanup around the workspace deletion; the failure is logged and the deletion continues as the message says.
checkWorkers catches the queue query and returns with no log at all, so the watcher silently stops reporting whether any microservices worker is connected.
The catch is narrow: the documented race where the directory is no longer empty is ignored and any other error is warned about.
The cancellation state machine reports canceled/errored through the returned state and the empty catch handlers only suppress unhandled rejections on the optional complete promise.
The caught JSON.parse is a probe: when the data is not JSON the raw string is kept and used, so nothing is lost.
The function is documented to return undefined when the lookup is inconclusive, so the null-ish answer is the explicit unknown result the caller must handle.
A failed content-type probe is logged and the code falls back to the png proxy URL, which still produces a working logo.
The catch rethrows unless Stripe is mid identity verification, where the wallet lookup is expected to fail and the stored address is used with a warning.
The probe already swallowed per-URL failures before this edit and still does; the edit only swaps fetch for the guarded helper.
The old catch logged and returned an empty array; the edit rethrows a DatabaseError so a failed query no longer reads as a contact in no segments.
The comment states it fails open on purpose because the value only labels the support chat; the error is logged and the page is not broken.
An unserializable message returns null, which the comparison treats as different on purpose, and the null is an explicit signal rather than a fabricated match.
The edit only wraps the existing loader in telemetry; no error handling in the scope changed.
The enqueue failures were already caught and logged before; the edit only lowers the level from error to warn, so the scope still logs and continues and the concern remains.
The change sanitizes the connector error data before it reaches the client; existing error paths still throw.
The edit adds two SQLSTATE codes that become thrown RequestErrors, not swallows.
Only the comment about the audit plugin names changed; no code was touched.
Both new catches wrap the failure in a thrown Error, so the caller still receives it.
A failing redis options decode is turned into a thrown Error, and the function that is now cached does not swallow anything.
The regenerated wrapper keeps the try/catch that rethrows the error after logging.
The route rethrows the domain and validation errors and wraps anything else in a DubApiError.
